summary: Explains why RFC 1240, which provided OSI connectionless transport services on top of UDP, should be moved to historic status. It was published as a Proposed Standard but had no known implementations, and there was growing concern about UDP-based transports where congestion can occur.

plainLanguage.summary: An old rule that nobody was using needed retiring. This document explains why it is being put away.

subtitle: Explaining why an old and unused RFC should be retired.

tldr.problem: RFC 1240, which defined OSI connectionless transport services running over UDP, was published as a Proposed Standard but never implemented and faced concerns about UDP-based transports in congested networks.
tldr.mechanism: This applicability statement documents the technical and practical reasons for moving RFC 1240 to Historic status, arguing that the benefits of using UDP do not justify the complexity and congestion control risks.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1240 is moved to Historic status, discouraging new implementations and signaling that TCP-based OSI transport is the preferred alternative.

today: RFC 2556 is an Informational RFC published in March 1999, stating that RFC 1240 is Historic. RFC 1240 remains Historic and is not recommended for new implementations.

sections.title: RFC 1240 and the Lack of Adoption
sections.content: RFC 1240 defined how to run OSI (Open Systems Interconnection) connectionless transport services on top of UDP. Published in June 1991 as a Proposed Standard, it was intended to provide an alternative transport mechanism. However, no known implementations of RFC 1240 were ever developed or deployed. A survey of the IETF community in October 1998 found no evidence of current use, and responses from relevant organizations, including ISO itself, supported moving the RFC to Historic status.
sections.plainLanguage: A rule for how to send messages using an older system was written down, but nobody ever actually used it. After checking, the Internet community decided it was not needed.

sections.title: Congestion Control Concerns
sections.content: Since RFC 1240 was published, significant experience with Internet congestion control has accumulated. UDP-based transport protocols are problematic because implementers often create their own reliability and congestion control functions that may not incorporate modern understanding of congestion management. This creates a risk of congestion collapse. RFC 1240's architecture, which assumes reliability algorithms would reside in the higher-level OSI protocols, does not adequately address these modern concerns.
sections.plainLanguage: Fast delivery is tempting, but without proper care, it can actually slow down the whole network when everyone tries to send at once. The old rule did not worry enough about this problem.

sections.title: Moving to Historic Status
sections.content: Given the complete lack of deployment experience and the known risks of UDP-based transports in congested environments, RFC 1240 is reclassified as Historic. Implementers are encouraged to use TCP-based approaches instead, as RFC 2126 describes. This decision reflects the principle that standards should reflect actual or anticipated use and that transport choices must account for modern Internet realities.
sections.plainLanguage: The Internet community decided to officially say: this rule is not good anymore, and we encourage people to use a better method instead.

references.text: Shue, C., Haggerty, W. and K. Dobbins, "OSI connectionless transport services on top of UDP: Version 1.", RFC 1240, June 1991.
Pouffary, Y. and A. Young, "ISO Transport Service on top of TCP (ITOT)", RFC 2126, March 1997.
